st.t: Evaluation design: Preferences differ from professional correctness
st.an: The excerpt is bibliography-only. Although it cites work on agent benchmarks, evaluation frameworks, contamination and evaluation awareness, it provides no substantive NIST findings or argument indicating whether answer quality, human preference and professional workflow success require distinct evaluation designs.

st.t: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
st.an: The excerpt is only a bibliography. Although it cites work on real-world agent benchmarks and evaluation frameworks, it provides no attributable NIST argument, findings or recommendations on whether professional-task realism complicates reproducible scoring.

st.t: Agent benchmarks: Protocol scores are not competence
st.an: NIST materially develops the cluster’s proposition by specifying how repeated trials trade evaluation cost against quantified sampling uncertainty and by treating LLM-judge quality as a separate determinant of score meaning. Its guidance reinforces that protocol scores require uncertainty-aware design and independently scrutinised automated grading.
qs: Having models attempt each item multiple times increases evaluation cost but can reduce uncertainty of evaluation results and enable an evaluator to quantify what portion of the uncertainty stems from model sampling.
Because the results of the evaluations are determined solely by the LLM-judge, the design and quality of the judge can have a significant impact on the meaning of evaluation results.

st.t: Evaluation validity: Benchmark safeguards impose trade-offs
st.an: NIST accepts that benchmark results are bounded and cannot alone establish real-world performance or safety, then materially develops the proposition with purpose-specific guidance on construct definition, valid inference, reproducibility, contamination controls, realistic baselines, cost considerations and complementary human or field evaluation. Its scope is narrower than the cluster because it addresses using existing automated benchmarks rather than broader governance or benchmark development.
qs: The design, execution, and reporting of an evaluation all depend on the evaluation objectives, including what should be measured (the measurement construct) and intended uses for the results produced.
Comprehensive: conducting evaluations via multiple methods and modalities (e.g., automated benchmarking, human red-teaming, field testing, etc.) may be more expensive but can improve assurance.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: NIST accepts the cluster’s premise that capability is task- and context-specific and materially develops its evaluation implications. It provides concrete practices for testing whether benchmarks represent intended constructs and deployment conditions, quantifying uncertainty, preserving reproducibility, and preventing benchmark results from being overgeneralised into claims of general competence or real-world value. It does not directly address legal workflow redesign, verification of particular outputs, or labour effects.
qs: Report assumptions or evidence for the relationship between performance on the evaluated benchmark and the intended measurement construct (see Practice 1.2).
Use caution when making claims that generalize evaluation results beyond the scope of the intended measurements as established in Practice 1.2.

st.t: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
st.an: NIST supports the cluster’s core proposition that benchmark results should not be treated as self-sufficient evidence of real-world suitability. Its recommendation to compare results with similar evaluations, other evidence and existing knowledge reinforces contextualised assurance, though the excerpt does not address workplace outcomes or broader governance mechanisms.
qs: Discuss the degree to which evaluation results agree or disagree with similar evaluations or other relevant evidence and existing knowledge.

kp.k: Draft offers voluntary guidance, not settled measurement standards
kp.d: The January 2026 initial public draft presents preliminary practices for automated benchmark evaluations of language models and AI agent systems. It addresses selecting and implementing existing benchmarks, rather than benchmark creation or organizational evaluation governance. Its contribution is cross-domain measurement guidance, not evidence about changes in legal services; relatively immature practices are explicitly identified as emerging.
qs: This draft provides voluntary practices for automated benchmark evaluations of language models and AI agent systems.
The document provides practices to implement and report on existing benchmarks to meet organizational needs, rather than practices to create new benchmarks.
The practices presented in this document are intended to reflect best practices; where relevant, practices that are relatively less mature in ecosystem use are labeled as emerging practice.

kp.k: Automated benchmarks cannot satisfy every evaluation objective
kp.d: The draft distinguishes structured, verifiable, stable tasks suitable for automated benchmarking from open-ended, dynamic, human-interactive or process-oriented tasks better addressed through other methods. It identifies red teaming, human-subject experiments, field testing and post-deployment monitoring as alternatives or complements, and notes that multiple methods can improve assurance at greater expense.
qs: Not all evaluation objectives can be met by automated benchmark evaluations.
This report is scoped to automated benchmark evaluations—evaluations that, once set up, can be run without any additional human input.
Comprehensive: conducting evaluations via multiple methods and modalities (e.g., automated benchmarking, human red-teaming, field testing, etc.) may be more expensive but can improve assurance.

kp.k: Evaluation objectives must determine benchmark selection
kp.d: Evaluators should document what they intend to measure and how results will be used before selecting benchmarks. The draft distinguishes abstract properties from downstream outcomes, and average-case from best- or worst-case behavior. Benchmark relevance may rest on direct measurement, a conceptual relationship or evidence of downstream predictive correlation; these are different grounds for interpretation, not interchangeable demonstrations of capability.
qs: Clearly document exactly what each benchmark is expected to measure and how it relates to the evaluation objectives before conducting the evaluation, similar to scientific preregistration.
The benchmark directly measures the construct of interest.
The benchmark is conceptually related to the evaluation objective.
The benchmark predicts downstream outcomes of interest.

kp.k: Task format and coverage limit capability claims
kp.d: Benchmark selection should examine subject matter, difficulty, item format, grading, coverage and baseline quality. The draft cautions that multiple-choice formats simplify implementation but may poorly represent actual LLM use. GPQA is presented as measuring graduate-level multiple-choice question answering in biology, chemistry and physics, rather than unrestricted scientific competence. Appropriate difficulty depends on whether the objective is comparison, threshold assessment or representative average performance.
qs: Test items should reflect intended use cases.

This question format simplifies benchmark implementation but sacrifices validity for many evaluation aims, as most tasks that LLMs are used for in practice, such as a chatbot answering user questions are more akin to free-response than multiple-choice.
If the objective is to compare model performance during development, then a benchmark that is either too hard or too easy to the point of saturating is not useful.

kp.k: Contamination can inflate scores without transferable performance
kp.d: The draft warns that training on benchmark contents or formats can produce higher scores through spurious relationships rather than performance transferable to unseen data. It recommends considering item diversity, sample size and statistical power, alongside contamination risks. Keeping benchmark data hidden during training or generating it after system creation can reduce contamination; canary strings are identified as an emerging check for blatant training on test data.
qs: If systems are trained to solve specific benchmark contents or formats, evaluation results may become “contaminated” — systems may take advantage of spurious relationships in the benchmark data to score higher than they would on unseen data in practice.
Contamination risk can be reduced by efforts to keep benchmark data hidden during training or by using benchmark data generated after the system was created.
Statistical power analysis can support this determination.

kp.k: Performance depends on protocols, scaffolding and resource budgets
kp.d: The draft treats measured performance as dependent on inference settings, agent scaffolding, tools, environments, instructions and scoring choices. Protocols should prioritize evaluation objectives while considering comparability, external validity, cost control and, where appropriate, performance optimization. Agent evaluations need explicit stopping conditions. Sensitivity analyses and tool-ablation experiments can reveal how protocol design affects results, while optimization on a separate development set reduces test-set overfitting risk.
qs: A given benchmark can generally be implemented in many different ways.
The most important principle of evaluation protocol design is that procedures should be designed to support the objectives of the evaluation (Practice 1.1). This principle overrides all others.
Agent scaffolding defines exactly how a model is turned into an agent.
Agents with larger budgets generally have higher performance, though this effect varies by model and domain.

kp.k: Cost-performance reporting is essential for meaningful comparisons
kp.d: The draft identifies cost control and joint cost-performance reporting as emerging practices. Higher execution expenditure can increase performance, making a single score misleading when systems receive unequal resources. Comparability can be supported either by uniform cost controls or by reporting costs alongside performance. For estimating real-world utility, evaluation expenditure should resemble deployment expenditure; cost-performance curves can expose trade-offs hidden by headline rankings.
qs: This is because the performance of language models and general-purpose AI systems can often be increased by running them in higher-execution-cost modes.

Otherwise, if uniform cost-controls are not implemented, a downstream user may be able to obtain higher downstream utility with a cheaper but seemingly lower-performing model run in a higher-execution-cost mode.

Uniform cost-controls across models are not strictly necessary though—if one is willing to report both costs and performance alongside each other, then comparability is valid even if different systems incur different costs.

kp.k: Automated judges require grading quality assurance
kp.d: Where responses cannot be graded programmatically, an LLM judge may determine evaluation results, making judge quality consequential to what scores mean. Emerging recommendations include comparison against human grading, multiple judges, interrater agreement and careful prompt testing. Separately, brittle answer parsers can reject answers a human would regard as correct; the draft suggests LLM-assisted parsing as one possible remedy, not as a guarantee of reliable grading.
qs: Because the results of the evaluations are determined solely by the LLM-judge, the design and quality of the judge can have a significant impact on the meaning of evaluation results.
However, such parsers can be brittle, as sometimes models can output answers that are technically correct when checked by a human but which the parser is unable to handle.
When using LLM judges for transcript review, evaluators should consider checking that these judges’ decisions match human judges’ decisions.

kp.k: Implementation failures can masquerade as capability limitations
kp.d: The draft identifies degraded model serving, tool-call errors, unsolvable task environments and safeguards as possible influences on measured performance. It recommends manual and automated transcript review, task review, deterministic solutions for complex environments, and comparison against existing evidence. Differences from published scores warrant investigation rather than automatically establishing invalidity. Versioning, complete logs and sandboxing also support interpretation, reproducibility and execution security.
qs: Automated benchmark evaluations can have bugs in their code or mistakes in their evaluation protocols.
It is common for these environments to have bugs (e.g., networking issues, broken dependencies, file permissions, etc.) that make certain items unsolvable.
A powerful technique for quality assurance of automated benchmark evaluations is to manually review evaluation transcripts to detect and diagnose bugs and mistakes.
Any test item whose deterministic solution does not successfully solve the task is likely to have some task configuration issue.

kp.d: The draft distinguishes solution contamination during evaluation from grader gaming, where a system exploits scoring loopholes rather than completing the intended task. Flexible coding tools make agentic evaluations especially exposed. In CAISI's reported CVE-Bench implementation, internet access supported realistic workflows but transcript review revealed searches for answers using command-line tools. CAISI changed the system prompt; the draft describes disabling internet access while supplying tools and documentation upfront as a more robust longer-term solution.
qs: Evaluation cheating occurs when a model has an opportunity to solve a test item in an unintended way that undermines its measurement validity.
Cheating is more likely to occur on agentic evaluations, where models often have access to flexible coding tools that can enable potentially unwanted solution paths.
However, via automated transcript review, CAISI discovered that models sometimes used command line tools like curl to search the web for answers to test items.
In the longer run, a more robust solution would be to disable internet access while providing more tools and documentation up front.

kp.k: Evaluation awareness complicates generalization to real-world behavior
kp.d: Citing recent research, the draft reports that evaluation cues can influence behavior in certain models, creating an external-validity concern. Verbalized recognition of being evaluated is one detectable form, but detecting and quantifying evaluation awareness more generally remains an open research problem. The draft recommends discussing its possible effects and, where relevant, reporting rates of verbalized awareness rather than treating benchmark behavior as necessarily representative of deployment.
qs: Recent work has shown that for certain models, model behavior can be influenced by cues that the input is part of an evaluation exercise [12][13][14].
The sensitivity to these cues is a challenge to external validity, since such cues are unlikely to be present during real-world use.
Developing more general solutions to detect and quantify the effect of evaluation awareness is an open line of research.

kp.k: Uncertainty analysis must match intended interpretations
kp.d: The draft recommends specifying statistical analysis in advance, reporting modeling assumptions and choosing aggregate metrics aligned with objectives. It distinguishes uncertainty arising from nondeterministic model completions from uncertainty associated with sampling benchmark items, and recommends separating sources where possible. Unmodeled influences such as prompt formats should be disclosed. Statistical comparisons should account for appropriate uncertainty and effect sizes; aggregation should not arbitrarily combine distinct constructs.
qs: It is good practice to define a statistical analysis procedure in advance of implementing and running the evaluation, in conjunction with the task setting specification practices described in Sections 1 and 2.
If evidence suggests that the benchmark measures multiple constructs, then care should be taken that aggregate metrics do not combine these measurements in an arbitrary manner.
Ideally, different sources of variation should be decomposed and reported separately.
However, statistical test results should be interpreted probabilistically and considered alongside effect size.

kp.k: CAISI examples illustrate procedures rather than universal findings
kp.d: The draft uses CAISI's 2025 model evaluations to illustrate implementation and reporting. Its GPQA example uses all 198 GPQA-Diamond questions; its CVE-Bench example uses 15 items and 4 trials per task, with a 500,000 weighted input/output token agent budget. For GPQA analysis, CAISI reports average accuracy and standard errors estimated with a generalized linear mixed model. These examples concern specific science and cybersecurity benchmarks and do not establish profession-wide or legal-service performance.
qs: Number of samples: all 198 GPQA-Diamond questions
Number of test items and trials per task: 15 items and 4 trials per task.
Agent budget: 500,000 “weighted” input/output tokens
CAISI reported average accuracy across the full benchmark with a standard error of the mean estimated using a generalized linear mixed model.
These standard errors account for LLM sampling and finite benchmark size.

kp.k: Transparency and qualified claims support responsible interpretation
kp.d: The draft recommends reporting objectives, benchmark and model versions, protocol choices, statistical assumptions, uncertainty and relevant baseline conditions. Item-level results, transcripts and evaluation code can aid replication and diagnosis, subject to business, security and contamination concerns. Claims should distinguish observations, inferences, predictions and normative statements, explain evidence connecting benchmarks to intended constructs or downstream outcomes, and avoid unsupported generalization beyond measurement scope.
qs: Sharing evaluation details and evaluation data such as test transcripts increases reproducibility and enables others to draw their own determinations about what results imply, though transparency must be weighed against business and security concerns.
Differentiate observations, inferences, predictions, and normative statements.
State assumptions or cite evidence supporting any usage of evaluation results to predict future measurements.
Use caution when making claims that generalize evaluation results beyond the scope of the intended measurements as established in Practice 1.2.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: NIST/CAISI makes cross-domain claims about automated AI benchmarking, not claims about legal services: benchmarks can support model selection and deployment decisions, but performance depends on evaluation design and need not generalize to real-world use.
pts.d: The draft claims that automated benchmarks may be cheaper and faster than other evaluation methods, while multimethod evaluation can improve assurance. It states that increasing reasoning effort or agent budgets generally improves performance at greater computational cost, with effects varying by model and domain; consequently, performance rankings without cost context can mislead users about utility. It also identifies training contamination, agents obtaining answers or exploiting graders, and models responding to evaluation cues as threats to measurement validity. Reporting protocols, uncertainty, costs, and transcripts is presented as supporting reproducibility and interpretation. These are methodological claims and recommendations, rather than forecasts of occupational replacement or legal-market change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis combines CAISI evaluation experience, concrete debugging examples, cited research, and measurement-science guidance; the draft does not provide a new quantitative demonstration for every recommendation.
pts.d: NIST/CAISI explicitly grounds the document in its industry-partner evaluations and measurement research. Examples from CAISI's 2025 DeepSeek evaluation include GPQA answer-format problems detected through manual transcript review and CVE-Bench agents searching online for benchmark answers detected through automated review. The draft illustrates statistical reporting with GPQA standard errors accounting for model sampling and finite benchmark size, and illustrates cost-performance reporting with CVE-Bench trajectories. Research references support claims about search-time contamination and evaluation awareness. General claims about cost savings, transparency, and assurance are offered as methodological guidance rather than quantified effect estimates. The document labels less mature practices as emerging.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The January 2026 initial public draft presents provisional, voluntary practices for current evaluation work, without a dated forecast of future AI capabilities.
pts.d: The scope is existing automated benchmarks that can run without additional human input once configured, principally for measuring capabilities. The draft cautions that automated benchmarking does not meet every evaluation objective, especially where tasks are dynamic, subjective, or require interaction with people. Generalization depends on benchmark fit, deployment-like conditions, credible baselines, protocol settings, and statistical assumptions. Increased execution resources do not improve every model or domain equally. Evaluation-awareness detection remains an open research problem. Transparency recommendations are qualified by business, security, and contamination concerns.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are AI evaluators, developers, and deployers; downstream beneficiaries include procurement officers, integrators, business decision-makers, and end consumers.
pts.d: Technical teams in companies, government, academia, and third-party evaluation organizations are expected to apply the practices when selecting benchmarks, implementing protocols, debugging systems, and reporting results. Consumers of evaluation reports may better understand model suitability, comparative performance, resource costs, and limitations. Federal agencies are a stated policy audience for the guidelines and resources. No legal occupation, law-firm segment, legal client group, or access-to-justice population is specifically identified, and no legal-sector effects should be inferred from this source.
